methodology: Sampled 10 of the 100 apps, spanning every confidence band (high/medium/low) and both easy self-serve apps and the hardest gated/ambiguous ones. For each, a real browser session (not the plain-HTTP crawler) visited the actual docs/marketing pages and every claimed field (auth method, self-serve-vs-gated verdict, API surface breadth) was checked by hand against what the page actually says. Corrections were applied directly back into data/results.json rather than kept as a separate 'known issues' list, so the shipped dataset reflects the post-verification, higher-accuracy pass -- not the first pass.

samples.name: Stripe
samples.detail: Verdict (self-serve-free, buildable) was right. Auth description was imprecise: said generic 'API key (Bearer)', actual primary scheme is HTTP Basic Auth with the key as username; Bearer is only the documented cross-origin alternative.

samples.name: GitHub
samples.detail: PAT/OAuth2 Bearer auth and free self-serve access confirmed exactly against docs.github.com.

samples.name: Slack
samples.detail: Free self-serve developer sandbox confirmed. Noted docs have migrated from api.slack.com to docs.slack.dev -- evidence URL still resolves via redirect.

samples.name: PitchBook
samples.detail: Verdict (contact-sales, not buildable) confirmed, but refined: PitchBook does sell a real Data Feed/API/CRM/LLM-partnership product -- it isn't that no API exists, it's that literally the only public CTA is a 'request a free trial' lead-gen form. Also noteworthy: our HTTP crawler got a 403 here, but a real browser was let through to the marketing page -- bot-blocking and 'no public docs' turned out to be two separate, coincidentally overlapping findings.

samples.name: DealCloud
samples.detail: Docs confirm word-for-word: an existing DealCloud admin must enable API capability for a user group before an API key can even be generated. No public signup path exists anywhere in the docs.

samples.name: Gladly
samples.detail: Docs assume 'your organization's Gladly domain' with no signup/trial CTA on the API reference page -- consistent with enterprise/contact-sales gating.

samples.name: Brex
samples.detail: Verdict (customer-gated, not buildable by outsiders) confirmed word-for-word: token generation requires signing in to dashboard.brex.com 'as an account admin or card admin.' Auth description corrected from generic 'OAuth2' to the actual mechanism: a dashboard-issued bearer user token, not a full OAuth2 authorization flow.

samples.name: Gumroad
samples.detail: First pass was wrong. The crawler followed the brief's own hint URL to a stale/redirecting help-center article that returned 19 characters, and we concluded the API was narrow and thinly documented (low confidence). The real docs live at app.gumroad.com/api and are broad -- Products, Sales, Subscribers, Licenses, Payouts, Media, Workflows, Custom fields -- and Gumroad ships an official CLI explicitly described as 'built for humans and AI agents alike.' Buildability corrected from yes-with-limits to yes; confidence corrected from low to high.

samples.name: iPayX
samples.detail: First pass treated this as an unverifiable, possibly-tiny/nonexistent product because docs.ai/docs returned near-empty content and web search surfaced an unrelated 'iPay' Africa/Jack Henry product family. On manual browse, ipayx.ai turned out to be a real, very new FINTRAC-registered FX-fee audit product whose homepage headline literally advertises 'Live in Claude MCP - n8n - Zapier' and a dedicated 'MCP Agent Developer' persona ('Connect via MCP SSE'). It is one of the most explicitly agent-native apps in the entire list -- and we almost wrote it off as noise. Still buildability=no because there is no public API/MCP reference doc to build against without creating an account, but confidence corrected from low to medium and the one-liner rewritten entirely.

samples.name: Paygent Connect
samples.detail: Confirmed a real Japanese payment-gateway company, Paygent (paygent.co.jp), exists: entirely sales-led (a 'request materials' / phone-inquiry model, typical of Japanese domestic payment processors), no public API docs, no self-serve signup -- consistent with our contact-sales/no-docs verdict. However we could not confirm this is the same product as the brief's specific 'Paygent Connect (NMI-powered)' hint, which reads like a possibly different, US-market white-label product. Left flagged as a genuine unresolved ambiguity rather than papered over.

accuracy.note: Post-verification accuracy is 100% BY CONSTRUCTION on this sample because every confirmed miss was corrected directly in data/results.json -- the number that matters is the miss rate we caught (50% of the sample needed some correction, 20% needed a real correction to the bottom-line verdict: Gumroad and iPayX), not a claim that the other 90 unsampled apps are error-free. Extrapolated, that implies a comparable share of the full 100 may still contain uncaught detail-level errors; the two categories most at risk are (a) apps whose crawl text was thin/redirected (same failure mode as Gumroad) and (b) very new/small vendors search doesn't index well (same failure mode as iPayX).
